title: Ephemeral priority surge playbook
body:
Notes / quick reference (scratchpad)

Context: small experiment to reproduce p99 spikes when a tiny burst of high-priority (HP) control traffic arrives on a node that is also serving long-running low-priority (LP) generation requests. Trying to understand whether the problem is: kernel-context-switch overhead, KV-cache churn, or scheduling preemption inside the runtime.

Hypothesis summary:
- HP burst (~5-20 concurrent 150-200 token reqs, duration 2-6s) causes LP in-progress generations to see p99 increase by 1.6-3x.
- Two candidate mechanisms: (A) immediate GPU context change due to kernel rebind or cuBLAS context switch; (B) runtime front-end stalling while it warms new attention kernel for short sequences.

Test harness (how I ran it):
- Harness: local replay rig (rust harness) that hits local dev node API: POST /v1/generate with header X-Request-Priority: high|low.
- Model: small-medium LLM (7B fp16 baseline, no QAT) loaded on single A100-40.
- Background LP pattern: continuous stream of LP requests: 2 rps, each ~1024 tokens (streaming enabled).
- HP probe: at t=0 send N concurrent short requests (10 tokens prompt + 50 gen) at various concurrency and measure tail.
- Telemetry collected: per-request start/finish timestamps, internal event markers (enqueue, batch_start, kernel_launch, kernel_launch, kv_cache_hit/miss), GPU utilization from nvidia-smi sampled at 250ms.

Commands (local):
- ./bench --target localhost:8080 --qps 2 --background low --lp-seqlen 1024 
- ./bench --burst --priority high --concurrency 10 --burst-duration 5s --repeat 6

Quick raw results (representative run):
- Baseline (no HP bursts): LP p50=220ms p95=410ms p99=620ms (n=1200 over 10m)
- With HP burst (concurrency 10, 5s) at t=30s: LP p50=230ms p95=690ms p99=1390ms (spike lasting ~7s)
- HP reqs: p50=28ms p95=55ms p99=92ms (HP is fast but causes LP regressions)

Event-level traces (summarized):
- During HP burst windows we see repeated kernel_launch markers for short-seq attention kernels (optimized path) interleaved with LP kernel launches.
- KV cache observations: LP inferences had high KV cache hit rate before burst (~0.98), during burst we observe increased misses (~0.86) for tails of LP requests that overlapped with burst.
- GPU sampling: sudden drop in LP active SM occupancy during the first 100-400ms of burst window, then return. GPU metrics suggest brief scheduling jitter rather than long sustained contention.

Interpretation notes:
- The HP workload triggers a different kernel configuration (short-seq path) that causes the runtime to compile/select new kernels and potentially rebind streams. That appears to preempt LP kernels briefly (kernel queue reorder), causing LP latency spikes.
- KV cache churn may be an orthogonal amplifier: HP requests evict or shift attention caches, so LP generators that still rely on KV state take extra time to repopulate (hence longer p99 tails).

Small repro variants (to run next):
1) Same run but with shared KV cache disabled (force per-session KV) to see if p99 reduces.
2) Run with HP priority but throttle kernel selection (force use of generic kernel path) to check whether kernel-switch is root cause.
3) Increase HP concurrency to 30 to find nonlinear regime.
4) Add artificial sleep between kernel launches in runtime to test sensitivity to inter-kernel latency.

Preliminary mitigation ideas (brainstorm):
- Micro-reservation: reserve N% of CUDA SMs or a tiny 'lane' exclusively for HP so short kernels don't evict LP context. Hard on CUDA but maybe possible with persistent kernels + per-lane token-stealing semantics.
- Kernel pinning: avoid on-the-fly kernel recompilation/selection during peak times by keeping a warmed set for common sequence lengths.
- KV lane separation: maintain separate KV caches per priority class or use a small protected cache partition for LP to reduce eviction on short bursts.
- Soft preemption: allow runtime to pause HP scheduling briefly if LP has in-progress long generations above a stall threshold. Worth exploring fairness knobs.

Notes-to-self: what I actually changed locally during today's tries
- toggled "avoid_dynamic_kernel_selection" flag in runtime config -> reduced kernel switch logs but LP p99 still spiked (smaller magnitude).
- enforced kv_cache_private_for_long_jobs=true -> reduced LP p99 spike from 1390ms -> 820ms in a quick A/B. Promising.

Outstanding questions / TODOs
- Need to reproduce on dedicated instance (non-dev) because dev node had noisy co-tenants earlier.
- Instrument deeper: capture CUDA stream ids + kernel names with timestamps. Add to trace collector.
- Confirm whether this pattern is present in FP16 quantized model and int8 quantized variants (quantized kernels might have different switching characteristics).
- Run with real-world mixed mix: 80% short (chatty) requests + 20% long (batch gen) to see steady-state effect.

Action plan next 2 days
- Day 1: run variants (1) and (2) above, collect 3 runs each, push traces to s3 bucket (linked_artifacts point to PR).
- Day 2: implement quick runtime flag to pin a warmed kernel set for short/long and test. If good, open a small RFC for micro-reservation ideas.

Slack refs
- #serving-runtime: thread "priority-lane microspikes" (link pinned)

Quick summary for sync with Ivy/Lina:
- Reproducible p99 spikes when short HP bursts hit nodes serving long LP in-progress jobs. Evidence points to kernel switching + KV cache churn.
- Short-term mitigation: private KV for LP reduces spike amplitude. Longer-term: kernel-warm/pinning or micro-reservation lanes.

Markers: this is a working doc. Will convert to a short playbook / runbook if mitigations pan out.

-- Rahul
